lead: A solid-state microwave source turns DC into RF inside a small piece of semiconductor, with no vacuum and no heated cathode. Each one relies on negative resistance: over part of its range, more voltage gives less current, so the device feeds energy into a resonant circuit instead of taking it. The Gunn diode gets it from electrons moving between energy valleys, the IMPATT and TRAPATT diodes from an avalanche and a transit delay, and the tunnel diode from quantum tunnelling. They are small, need a few volts to about a hundred volts, and serve in radar front ends, police speed guns, motion sensors and local oscillators.
prereq: You need: p–n junctions and reverse breakdown, drift velocity and mobility, and cavity resonators (see Microwave resonators and Q factor).

blocks.text: A Gunn diode is a slab of n-type GaAs (or InP) of length L with ohmic contacts at both ends. It has no p–n junction: it is a transferred-electron device (TED). The conduction band of GaAs has a low central valley, where electrons are light and fast (mobility about 8500 cm²/V·s), and a satellite valley about 0.3 eV higher, where they are heavy and slow.

At low field all electrons sit in the central valley and the drift velocity rises with field. Above a threshold field of about 3.2 kV/cm, electrons gain enough energy to move to the satellite valley, so the average velocity falls as the field rises. A falling velocity means a falling current: negative differential resistance (NDR). At still higher fields the velocity levels off near 10⁷ cm/s.

A uniform field in the NDR region is unstable. A small region of high field (a domain) forms near the cathode, grows, drifts to the anode at about the saturated velocity, and is absorbed; then the next one forms. Each domain arrival gives a current pulse, so the current oscillates at the transit-time frequency.

blocks.where: f in hertz, v<sub>d</sub> the domain drift velocity (about 10⁵ m/s) and L the active length in metres. A 10 µm slab oscillates near 10 GHz.

items: Transit-time mode: needs n₀L > 10¹² cm⁻² (n₀ = doping in cm⁻³, L in cm) so that domains can form; frequency fixed by L.
Delayed and quenched domain modes: a resonant circuit sets the frequency a little below or above vd/L by delaying or quenching domain formation.

LSA mode (limited space-charge accumulation): the field swings through the NDR region faster than a domain can form, for 2 × 10⁴ < n₀/f < 2 × 10⁵ s/cm³; frequency set by the cavity, not by L, so higher frequency and power are possible.

blocks.text: The diode sits in a cavity that fixes the frequency; a varactor or YIG sphere tunes it. Output is milliwatts to about a watt, at a few per cent efficiency.

An IMPATT (impact-ionisation avalanche transit-time) diode is a reverse-biased junction held at breakdown, for example the Read structure p⁺–n–i–n⁺: a thin avalanche region followed by a drift region of length L<sub>d</sub>. Negative resistance comes from two delays that add up to half a cycle:

items: Avalanche delay: the carrier current in the avalanche keeps growing as long as the RF voltage is above breakdown, so it peaks a quarter cycle (90°) after the voltage peak.

Transit delay: the injected carrier pulse crosses the drift region at the saturated velocity v<sub>s</sub> and is designed to take about another quarter cycle at the terminals, so the terminal current lags the voltage by about 180°.
A current 180° out of phase with the voltage means negative resistance: the diode delivers RF power to the circuit.

blocks.where: v<sub>s</sub> ≈ 10⁵ m/s in silicon and L<sub>d</sub> the drift length in metres; a 5 µm drift region gives about 10 GHz.

blocks.text: IMPATTs give the most power of any solid-state source at millimetre waves, with efficiency typically several per cent up to about 15 %, but the avalanche makes them noisy. TRAPATT (trapped plasma avalanche triggered transit) is a large-signal mode of a similar diode: a voltage pulse drives an avalanche front across the whole diode, filling it with a dense electron-hole plasma that drops the voltage to a low value, and the plasma is then extracted slowly. Because the extraction takes much longer than the IMPATT transit time, TRAPATTs run at lower frequencies (below about 10 GHz), in pulses, with high efficiency (tens of per cent). A BARITT diode injects carriers over a forward-biased barrier by punch-through instead of avalanche: much lower noise, much lower power.

sections.h3: Tunnel diode and choosing a source

blocks.text: A tunnel diode is a p–n junction doped so heavily that its depletion layer is only about 10 nm thick, so electrons tunnel through the barrier. Its current rises to a peak I<sub>p</sub> at voltage V<sub>p</sub>, falls to a valley I<sub>v</sub> at V<sub>v</sub>, then rises again as an ordinary diode. Between V<sub>p</sub> and V<sub>v</sub> the slope is negative.

Bias the diode at a DC voltage between Vp and Vv, inside the negative-slope region, and connect a resonator: it oscillates. Tunnelling is very fast, so the device works at high frequency, but the voltage swing is a few tenths of a volt, so the power is only microwatts to milliwatts. Tunnel diodes serve as low-power oscillators, fast switches and low-noise amplifiers.

examples.question: A GaAs Gunn diode must oscillate in the transit-time mode at 10 GHz. Take v<sub>d</sub> = 10⁷ cm/s and a threshold field of 3.2 kV/cm. Find (a) the active length, (b) the threshold voltage, (c) the field at a bias of 8 V, (d) the least doping for the transit-time mode, and (e) the efficiency if the diode draws 0.5 A at 8 V and gives 100 mW of RF.
steps: L = v<sub>d</sub>/f = 10⁵ m/s ÷ 10¹⁰ Hz = 10⁻⁵ m = 10 µm.
Threshold voltage = E<sub>th</sub> × L = 3.2 × 10⁵ V/m × 10⁻⁵ m = 3.2 V.
At 8 V the field is 8 V/10⁻³ cm = 8 kV/cm, inside the NDR region (above 3.2 kV/cm).
Transit-time mode needs n₀L > 10¹² cm⁻². With L = 10⁻³ cm: n₀ > 10¹² ÷ 10⁻³ = 10¹⁵ cm⁻³.
DC input = 8 × 0.5 = 4 W; η = 0.1/4 = 0.025 = 2.5 %. The other 3.9 W heats the diode, so it needs a heat sink.
examples.answer: L = 10 µm, threshold 3.2 V, 8 kV/cm at 8 V bias, n₀ above 10¹⁵ cm⁻³, efficiency 2.5 %.

examples.question: A silicon IMPATT diode (v<sub>s</sub> = 10⁵ m/s) is to work at 10 GHz. (a) Find the drift length. (b) What drift length is needed at 94 GHz? (c) If it is biased at 100 V and 50 mA and delivers 0.5 W, find its efficiency.
steps: f ≈ v<sub>s</sub>/(2L<sub>d</sub>), so L<sub>d</sub> = v<sub>s</sub>/(2f) = 10⁵/(2 × 10¹⁰) = 5 × 10⁻⁶ m = 5 µm.
At 94 GHz: L<sub>d</sub> = 10⁵/(2 × 94 × 10⁹) = 0.53 µm, so millimetre-wave IMPATTs are very thin.
Check: the transit time L<sub>d</sub>/v<sub>s</sub> = 50 ps is half the 100 ps period, as the formula intends.
examples.answer: L<sub>d</sub> = 5 µm at 10 GHz and 0.53 µm at 94 GHz; efficiency 10 %.

traps: Calling the Gunn diode a p–n junction device. It is a bulk n-type slab; its negative resistance comes from electrons transferring to the slow satellite valley.
Giving IMPATT the Gunn mechanism, or the reverse. IMPATT = avalanche plus transit delay in a reverse-biased junction; Gunn = field-driven valley transfer.
Saying TRAPATT runs at low frequency "because of harmonics". It runs below the IMPATT range because extracting the trapped plasma takes much longer than a transit time.
Biasing a tunnel diode by current. The DC voltage must lie between the peak voltage V<sub>p</sub> and the valley voltage V<sub>v</sub>.
Quoting tube-like efficiencies for diodes. Gunn sources give a few per cent; 25 % would be unrealistic.

quiz.q: Which effect gives a Gunn diode its negative resistance?
quiz.a: The transferred-electron effect: above about 3.2 kV/cm electrons move from the fast central valley to a slow satellite valley, so the average drift velocity falls as the field rises.

quiz.q: Why is a Gunn diode used with a cavity?
quiz.a: The cavity stores energy at one frequency, so the negative resistance builds a stable, clean oscillation there; it also allows delayed, quenched or LSA modes whose frequency differs from v<sub>d</sub>/L. A bare diode gives a poorly defined, weak output.

quiz.q: A Gunn diode has v<sub>d</sub> = 10⁷ cm/s and oscillates at 12 GHz in the transit-time mode. Find L.
Explain how an IMPATT diode shows negative resistance although its drift region is passive.
quiz.a: The avalanche current peaks a quarter cycle after the voltage peak; the drift transit adds about another quarter cycle. The terminal current therefore lags the voltage by about 180°, so the device returns power to the circuit: negative resistance.

quiz.q: Where on its I–V curve is a tunnel diode biased to oscillate?
quiz.a: At a DC voltage between the peak voltage V<sub>p</sub> and the valley voltage V<sub>v</sub>, where the slope of current against voltage is negative.

quiz.q: A tunnel diode has I<sub>p</sub> = 10 mA at V<sub>p</sub> = 0.06 V and I<sub>v</sub> = 1 mA at V<sub>v</sub> = 0.35 V. Find its average negative resistance.
For a 10 µm GaAs slab at 10 GHz, which doping range allows the LSA mode?
quiz.a: 2 × 10⁴ < n₀/f < 2 × 10⁵ s/cm³ with f = 10¹⁰ Hz gives 2 × 10¹⁴ < n₀ < 2 × 10¹⁵ cm⁻³.

beyond: Transistor oscillators in GaAs, GaN and SiGe, with frequency multipliers, now do most diode jobs, and 77 GHz car radars are single chips. Resonant-tunnelling diodes oscillate above 1 THz in research. Search for "resonant tunnelling diode terahertz" and "frequency multiplier chain".
